extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators, rhetoricians, legal advocates, and students of public speaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and delivering classical-style orations (legal pleading and public harangue), emphasizing rhetorical effects, learning, preparation, and delivery. Targets speakers who aim to persuade, please, and move assemblies or courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Mean / moderation of virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue in speaking consists in a just mediocrity; orators should pursue a balanced character, tempering affability with severity and severity with affability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the 'golden mean' — combine opposite virtues without excess. Example: temper affability with proper severity (Crassus) and affable condescension with a rigid air (Scaevola). Avoid extremes that spoil effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of logic and analytical method
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator must understand the art of logic: divide a whole into parts, accurately define indeterminate ideas, explain obscurities by clear interpretation, identify doubtful matters and distinguish degrees of probability, and use rules to judge truth and valid inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scientific/logical knowledge allows precise legal reasoning and orderly argumentation. It is essential for turning practical pleading into a disciplined science rather than loose advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive acquaintance with polite literature and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful speaker attaches himself to polite literature and attains an elegant manner of expression; literary training (Greek and Roman) improves style and substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study poets, historians, philosophy to enrich diction, examples, and allusion. Servius's writings are cited as evidence of how literature refines eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis of teachers' strengths and avoidance of their defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit from multiple instructors/styles by adopting their good qualities while avoiding their faults—e.g., combine the accuracy of Balbus with the quickness of Aquilius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn various methods and selectively integrate them so your style gains the virtues of both precision and dexterity without inheriting their weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and readiness for public debate
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator should always come prepared; readiness elevates audience expectation and reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be 'ready prepared for the combat'—a well-prepared opening meets the public's high expectations and establishes authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled physical delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation in bodily gestures and voice: avoid excessive movement, large variations of voice, stamping the foot; maintain composure and measured physical presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical restraint lends dignity and authority. Excessive motion or theatricality undermines credibility; be steady and moderate in action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate voice qualities: force, warmth, pathos, tempered humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Language and vocal expression should be forcible, sometimes warm and pathetic, with strokes of humour tempered by becoming dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine emotional force with decorum. Use humour to enliven but not to degrade seriousness; calibrate tone to preserve respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and facility with short periods (colons)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good orator is often concise: uses short, well-turned periods and members (Greek colons) to express ideas forcefully and neatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor brevity where it strengthens argument; precise, compact sentences can be more effective than long-winded periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility across types of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Orators should be effective in a wide range of causes—judicial, public, and private—demonstrating adaptability to different subject matters and forums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate breadth of practice; reputation as an orator is reinforced by success in many kinds of cases rather than specialization alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit between style and forum (judicial vs. public)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt style to the occasion: some speakers are better suited to judicial trials, others to public debate; choose and shape speech accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antonius is cited as better for judicial trials, Crassus for public harangues. Tailor tone, structure, and examples to the expectations of judges or a popular assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity, correctness, and elegant delicacy of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctness and purity of diction are marks of merit; an elegant, delicate style (attic qualities) enhances persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a refined vocabulary and polished phrasing. Avoid vulgar or provincial expressions unless strategically employed; prefer well-chosen examples and polished turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accent and pronunciation (native elegance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronunciation and a graceful accent (a native, well-bred manner of speaking) contribute to the charm and persuasive effect of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on articulation and local prosody; a pleasant native accent can add flavor and immediacy to delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning in allied disciplines (philosophy, jurisprudence, history)
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator's highest perfection comes from combining rhetorical skill with comprehensive knowledge of philosophy, law, and history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep subject-matter learning supplies material for argument and lifts oratory from technique to a more authoritative discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three primary effects of oratory: inform, please, move
rubrics_metrics.description: The orator must (1) inform the hearers, (2) please them, and (3) move their passions — these are the three things an orator should be able to effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate speech by whether it conveys clear information, engages and pleases the audience, and produces emotional movement that advances the speaker's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasing the people as central metric (public reception)
rubrics_metrics.description: An accomplished orator is judged by the people; pleasing the populace is a central proof of eloquence and typically aligns with the judgment of the learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to engage popular taste and secure public assent; public applause and emotional response are reliable indicators of rhetorical effectiveness (with caution about isolated false approvals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasiveness and winning assent
rubrics_metrics.description: Oratory should win the listeners' assent: make them credit, believe, and relish the force of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reasoning, examples, and style so that the audience adopts your position as true; failing to secure assent indicates ineffective argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliciting and managing a range of emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator must be able to provoke and regulate emotions—joy, grief, pity, shame, remorse, resentment, wonder, hope, fear—according to rhetorical aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speech rhythms and rhetorical moves to guide the audience through desired emotional responses; measure success by the audience's felt reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdotes, wit, and humour strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotes and witticisms can neutralize opposing arguments, change mood, and make serious points more palatable (e.g., Crassus's cock-boat story undermining Scaevola).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-chosen stories early to deflate opponent's strongest points, to charm the audience, or to reframe issues—always temper wit with dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedents, authorities, and multiple viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Support arguments by citing precedents, exhibiting a variety of views, and presenting authorities to strengthen and widen persuasive grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster claims with legal and historical precedents and examine the issue from several angles to convince both popular and learned audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful textual/legal exegesis vs. purposive interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish literal construction (the letter of a will or law) from the true intent or spirit; skillfully argue for the interpretation that best serves justice and common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate mastery over technical forms and the consequences of rigid literalism; show how arbitrary literalism would lead to absurd or unjust results when arguing for purposive readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long practice and accumulated experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive practice over many causes and years builds authority and rhetorical competence; longevity and repeated practice create seasoned orators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value experience: speakers with long careers and many trials command respect and practical skill not easily replaced by theoretical learning alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of declamatory, coarse, or illiterate manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a mere declaimer, ranter, or coarse, unpolished speaker is inferior to cultivated eloquence; refinement and learning distinguish true orators from mere loud speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rusticity, vulgarity, and abrasive coarseness. Cultivate polish, correctness, and learning to be taken seriously and to persuade elite and popular audiences alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in career strategy (choose competitions wisely)
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise speaker avoids unequal competitions and chooses the field where his strengths best serve him; strategic career and role choices reflect wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not engage opponents on ground where they have clear superiority. Build reputation by selecting causes and offices that fit your style and strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical diagnostic skill (understand how effects are produced)
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic or skilled orator can detect by what methods a speaker obtains or loses the true ends of speaking — i.e., identify the techniques that produce persuasive effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the ability to analyze rhetorical means (structure, device, tone) to reproduce successful effects and avoid weak devices; this analytical faculty refines speaking and teaching.
